content_preview.title: Rust 1.98.0 Ships Algebraic Floating-Point Methods and a Standard-Library Alternative to the itoa Crate
content_preview.summary: Rust 1.98.0 stabilizes non-deterministic algebraic float operations for faster loop vectorization and a format_into method that matches the itoa crate's performance.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The Rust project released version 1.98.0 on August 20, 2026, headlined by a set of "algebraic" floating-point methods that let the compiler reorder math operations for better performance, and a standard-library integer-formatting method built to replace the widely used `itoa` crate, according to the [Rust Blog](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/08/20/Rust-1.98.0/).

editor_notes.source_verification: All 3 sources fetched successfully (HTTP 200, no archive_fallback) and were read in full from the gzipped snapshots on disk, not re-fetched: source-0.html.gz (blog.rust-lang.org 'Announcing Rust 1.98.0', dated Aug. 20, 2026) confirms every direct quote used in the Overview and 'Algebraic floating-point methods' / 'A standard-library alternative to itoa' / 'ManuallyDrop and Box' sections verbatim, including the -ffast-math comparison, the a+b+c+d associativity example, the 'never cause undefined behavior' line, the format_into/NumBuffer description, the itoa-benchmark performance claim, and the RFC 3336 / Rust 1.96.0 ManuallyDrop history. source-1.html.gz (GitHub rust-lang/rust releases/tag/1.98.0) confirms the full Stabilized APIs list, both new lints (invalid_runtime_symbol_definitions, suspicious_runtime_symbol_definitions with the 'memcmp, memset, strlen' / 'planned to be expanded' language) and the c_void_returns lint, the two new Tier 3 targets and five ARM targets promoted to Tier 2 (all target triples match exactly), and the Compatibility Notes used in the article (repr(transparent) 'trivial' wording, derive(PartialOrd)/Ord fast-path warning, and the Emscripten WASM exception handling / -Zemscripten-wasm-eh=false removal, all quoted verbatim). Release timestamp on GitHub reads '20 Aug 18:05', consistent with the article's August 20, 2026 release date. source-2.html.gz (LinuxCompatible, byline Philipp Esselbach, published 2026-08-20 20:07) independently corroborates the algebraic-float non-determinism claim ('These methods are explicitly marked as non-deterministic. You will get slightly different results between builds.') and the format_into/itoa performance parity claim ('Benchmarks against itoa-benchmark show it runs on par with the crate itself.') verbatim as quoted in the article. No WebFetch fallback was needed; no snapshot failed.

editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Checked the specific technical claims flagged for extra scrutiny: (1) the five algebraic_* methods on f32/f64 and their non-deterministic-but-not-UB framing trace verbatim to the Rust Blog and are corroborated by LinuxCompatible; (2) format_into taking a &mut NumBuffer<Self> and matching itoa's benchmarked performance traces verbatim to the Rust Blog and is corroborated by LinuxCompatible's own code snippet; (3) the ManuallyDrop<Box<_>>/RFC 3336 stable-guarantee claim, including the Rust 1.96.0 fix date, traces verbatim to the Rust Blog. No wrong publication year appears anywhere in the article body — every date reference ('August 20, 2026', 'Rust 1.96.0', 'two releases earlier') is consistent across all three sources and with the actual snapshot timestamps (blog dated Aug. 20 2026, GitHub release dated 20 Aug 18:05, LinuxCompatible published 2026-08-20 20:07).
